title: Given two strings, find the length of the longest substring that appears in both, where a substring must be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Common Substring (Longest Contiguous Run Shared by Two Strings)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry holds the length of the common contiguous run ending at a given pair of positions: when the current characters match the entry is one plus the diagonal neighbour, and when they differ the entry resets to zero because contiguity is broken. We track the maximum entry. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared phrase suggests the two narrations came from the same automated source. Rajesh and Priya each have a narration, and the bank measures their longest shared run.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match the run extends from the diagonal by one, and on a mismatch it resets to zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry holds the length of the common contiguous run ending at a given pair of positions: when the current characters match the entry is one plus the diagonal neighbour, and when they differ the entry resets to zero because contiguity is broken. We track the maximum entry. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared phrase suggests the two narrations came from the same automated source. Rajesh and Priya each have a narration, and the bank measures their longest shared run.

**One line to remember:** On a match the run extends from the diagonal by one, and on a mismatch it resets to zero.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the table entry for positions i and j as the length of the longest common substring that ends exactly at character i of the first string and character j of the second string. When those two characters are equal, the run is one longer than the run ending at the previous pair, which is the diagonal cell, so the entry is one plus that diagonal value. When they differ, no common run can end here because a substring must be contiguous, so the entry resets to zero. The answer is the largest value anywhere in the table.

Bottom-up: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) { if (a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1)) { dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; best = Math.max(best, dp[i][j]); } else dp[i][j] = 0; }`. A concrete check: comparing SALARYPAY and MYSALARY, the longest shared run SALARY has length six. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, it differs sharply from the subsequence version because a mismatch resets rather than carrying forward, and a rolling two-row array reduces space to linear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared contiguous phrase is a strong signal that both narrations were produced by the same automated upstream system during a reconciliation check. Comparing all substrings directly is cubic or worse. This is exactly how the Longest Common Substring works: it finds the longest shared contiguous run in quadratic time with the extend-on-match, reset-on-mismatch recurrence.

The code defines a `NarrationCompareService` exposing `longestSharedRun(a, b)` returning the length of the longest common substring. A `Demo` runs it over two sample narrations and logs the length.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are SALARYPAY and MYSALARY. We want the longest contiguous run they share.

Step 1 — We align the first string down the rows and the second across the columns, starting every border cell at zero.

Step 2 — When we reach the S of SALARY in both strings, the characters match, so that cell becomes one plus its zero diagonal, giving one.

Step 3 — The next pair A and A match, so the cell becomes one plus the previous one, giving two. The run is building along the diagonal.

Step 4 — Continuing through L, A, R, Y each pair matches and the diagonal run grows to three, four, five, and six. The best value rises to six at the Y.

Step 5 — After SALARY the following characters diverge, so those cells reset to zero, and no later run reaches six. The answer is six, the length of SALARY. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:20:02 PM com.bank.narr.service.NarrationCompareService longestSharedRun
INFO: Longest shared narration run = 6
Oct 27, 2026 9:20:02 PM com.bank.narr.NarrationCompareApplication main
INFO: Longest shared contiguous phrase length is 6
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: a = "SALARYPAY", b = "MYSALARY"
    │
    ▼
  dp[i][j]: match → 1 + diagonal, mismatch → 0
    │ S==S → 1
    │ A==A → 2
    │ L,A,R,Y match → 3,4,5,6   (best=6)
    │ divergence → reset to 0
    ▼
  Output: longest shared run = 6  (SALARY)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern, and the mental model I use is a two dimensional grid where I align one string down the rows and the other across the columns. Each cell holds the length of the common contiguous run that ends exactly at that pair of characters. When the two characters match, the run is one longer than the diagonally previous run, so the cell is one plus the diagonal value. When they differ, contiguity is broken and the cell resets to zero.

Because a common substring can end anywhere, the answer is not in a corner but is the maximum value found anywhere in the table, which I track as I fill it. This runs in quadratic time and space, and I can drop the space to linear with two rolling rows. The point I always stress is that the reset on mismatch is what distinguishes the substring version from the subsequence version, where a mismatch carries the better neighbour forward instead of resetting.

At the National Bank of India I used this during reconciliation to compare two transaction narration strings and find the longest identical unbroken phrase, because a long shared contiguous phrase strongly suggested both narrations came from the same automated upstream system. I filled the run table and tracked the maximum. Explaining the extend-on-match, reset-on-mismatch recurrence, the fact that the answer is the table maximum rather than a corner, and the contrast with the subsequence version is what shows an interviewer I understand the Longest Common Substring pattern.
